summary: Comments on the on-line host name service proposals. It is related to RFCs 606, 608, 625 and 627.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 623 suggests ways to make a proposed host-name service more available and easier for programs to use. It recommends a backup copy, a binary format and a dedicated socket service instead of FTP.

questions: what backup did rfc 623 propose for the hostnames database
subtitle: Suggestions for reliable and easy access to a host-name database.

tldr.problem: A single host holding the official host-name database could be unavailable, and a retrieval method should be easy for programs to use.
tldr.mechanism: The author proposes a master copy at the NIC, a frequently updated secondary copy at another host, a machine-readable binary format and access through a dedicated program on its own socket.
tldr.outcome: RFC 623 offers design suggestions and volunteers UCSB as the secondary host; it does not announce that these proposals were implemented.

today: RFC 623 is a set of design suggestions for a proposed on-line host-name service.

sections.title: A Backup for the Master Database
sections.content:
Earlier proposals called for one host to maintain official host names and addresses, with the NIC implementing the database. The author notes that a single server might be unavailable when someone needs the data. Rather than asking every host to keep its own recent copy, he proposes that the NIC hold the master and one secondary host keep a copy updated at frequent intervals, such as once a day.

The author volunteers UCSB to serve as that secondary host.
sections.plainLanguage: A single host might be unavailable, so the author proposes keeping a second copy at another host. UCSB volunteers to hold that secondary copy.

sections.title: A Machine-Readable Binary Format
sections.content:
The proposal in progress called for an ASCII file. The author agrees that the database should be easy for programs to read and suggests binary records instead. In his example, a host address is an eight-bit number, a host name has a one-byte length followed by that many ASCII characters, and status attribute values are one-byte numbers.

He acknowledges that this format would be harder for people to read but argues that programs could interpret it more easily.
sections.plainLanguage: The author proposes binary records instead of an ASCII file so programs can process entries easily. He notes that the result would be less readable to people.

sections.title: A Dedicated Retrieval Service
sections.content:
RFC 608 proposed keeping the database as a file and retrieving it with FTP. The author questions whether FTP is suitable for this simple task and proposes a program running on its own socket at the NIC and the secondary host. That approach would avoid requiring a client to know the guest-account login parameters of each server.

The author invites comments on these proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of downloading the file through FTP, the author suggests a small program service at each host. Programs would not need to know different guest logins for the two sites.
